messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Khaled, a 56-year-old Middle Eastern man who had spent years managing social media campaigns from his apartment office and later from a small shared workspace downtown, first came to therapy after months of feeling unable to settle anywhere. The traumatic event he described was a late-night arrest two years earlier, when he was stopped outside a convenience store, pushed hard against the hood of a patrol car, and held in a choke of shouting, handcuffs, and bright headlights while officers searched him and ignored his attempts to explain that he had done nothing wrong. What stayed with him most was not only the fear but the humiliation: the taste of metal in his mouth from blood where he had bitten his tongue, the smell of asphalt and sweat, and the sense that the men in uniform who should have protected him could turn without warning. In the weeks after, he began to notice that the memory would arrive in fragments and he would push it away before he could fully see the scene in his mind. Sometimes, when a flash of it broke through, he felt a surge of intense rage, so sudden that he would tense his jaw and stop himself from thinking any further. He had come to believe that people were not what they seemed, that the world was a dangerous place, and that he had somehow acted against the kind of man he believed himself to be by not being able to prevent what happened. Those beliefs sharpened his sense that he could not trust appearances, and they made him wary in a way that spread into daily life. Because of what he had concluded about other people and about himself, he started avoiding anything that might stir up either painful feelings or, as he put it, “the wrong kind of relief.” He stopped watching television programs and films that showed police stops, protests, or even courtroom scenes, and he no longer read articles about similar events. He also became careful about where he stood in public: at cafés, in the office, and even in the supermarket he would instantly map exits, keep his back to walls, and scan faces and uniforms for signs of threat before he could feel comfortable enough to sit. Khaled described this constant checking as exhausting, but he felt he had no choice because once his mind told him the world was dangerous, he became unable to relax even in places he knew were safe. That state of alertness fed back into the way he interpreted other people, making every firm voice or brusque gesture feel like proof that people were not what they seemed, which deepened his conviction that trust was naïve and that he had been violated in a way that exposed something morally rotten in the world.

The pattern began to narrow his life. At work, where he monitored accounts and responded to client messages for much of the day, he found himself pausing at every notification sound, checking the office door, and choosing a seat nearest the exit during meetings. When he had to attend a client event or a crowded staff lunch, he would identify the quickest route out before he could concentrate on anything else. This vigilance kept him from being overtaken by feeling, but it also made any reminder of the arrest more potent; the more he avoided emotion, the more the memory seemed to return as a bodily shock, with the taste he remembered on his tongue and the rush of rage and shame that followed. He began to catch himself before the scene could fully form, pushing it away again, and the unfinished quality of those intrusions left him more unsettled. He noticed that the same effort to shut down feeling also left him colder toward his wife and children, who said he seemed distant and always on guard. Khaled interpreted that distance as evidence that something in him had changed for the worse, that he had not behaved as he should have and now could not fully inhabit the person he once was. That thought, in turn, intensified his suspicion of others and his sense that the world had become unpredictably unsafe, which made him scan even more closely and avoid even more completely. By the time he sought help, he was sleeping poorly, arranging his days around exits and threats, and feeling increasingly trapped by a life organized around staying ahead of the next shock. What brought him in was his fear that he was losing his family’s trust and his own sense of decency, and what he hoped for was some way to remember without being flooded by rage, dread, and the conviction that danger was waiting everywhere.
